key_concept: Mitochondria have a double membrane that divides the organelle into two aqueous compartments: the outer compartment (inter-membrane space) and the inner compartment, called the matrix, which is enclosed by the inner membrane.
steps: A mitochondrion is bounded by two membranes, an outer membrane and an inner membrane.
The space between the two membranes is the outer compartment, called the inter-membrane space.
The inner membrane forms infoldings called cristae and surrounds the inner compartment. This dense, homogeneous region is the matrix.
The matrix contains a single circular DNA molecule, a few RNA molecules, $70S$ ribosomes and the enzymes of the Krebs cycle.
So the inner mitochondrial membrane encloses the matrix, which is option (1).
why_not_others: Cytosol is the fluid of the cell outside the organelles, so it surrounds the mitochondrion rather than lying inside it. Mucus is an extracellular secretion, and aqueous humor is the fluid in the anterior chamber of the eye, so neither has anything to do with mitochondria.
common_trap: Students sometimes confuse the matrix with the inter-membrane space, or think of cytosol as the fluid inside every organelle.
time_saving_tip: Remember the sequence 'outer membrane → inter-membrane space → inner membrane (cristae) → matrix'. Mucus and aqueous humor are not cellular compartments at all, so you can eliminate them immediately.
